title: Representation and Verification of Domain-Based Application Service Identity within Internet PKI Using X.509 Certificates
summary: Specifies procedures for representing and verifying the identity of application services using X.509 certificates in the context of TLS, such as checking that a certificate really matches the server name the client meant to reach. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 9525.

eli5.summary: When you visit a website, your computer checks the ID card matches the name you typed. This document explains how to check it properly.

questions: how to verify server identity in tls certificate
what is a dns-id in a certificate
when to use the common name for hostname checks
subtitle: How a TLS client checks that a server's certificate really names the service it meant to reach, and how certificates should carry that name.

tldr.problem: Each application protocol had its own rules for putting a service's name into an X.509 certificate and for checking it, which confused certification authorities, developers and protocol designers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6125 defines reference and presented identifiers, tells CAs which identifier types to issue (DNS-ID first, CN-ID discouraged, wildcards discouraged), and gives clients an algorithm for matching them.
tldr.outcome: It was obsoleted by RFC 9525, so it describes an earlier generation of the rules for checking service identity.

today: RFC 6125 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9525, so use that for the current rules on checking service identity.

sections.title: Why Service Identity Needs Rules
sections.content:
When a client talks to an application service over TLS or DTLS, it has some idea of who it wants to reach (for example, "the website at example.com"). The server presents a public-key certificate issued by a certification authority (CA) under the Internet PKI using X.509 (PKIX). The RFC calls these the client's reference identity and the server's presented identity, and the client must check that they match in order to authenticate the communication.

Protocols had traditionally specified their own rules for this, and the divergence confused CAs, application developers and protocol designers. RFC 6125 codifies recommended procedures. Its main audience is protocol designers, who can reference it instead of defining their own rules. It does not supersede PKIX, which stays authoritative, and it covers only the name in the leaf server certificate, so clients still need to verify the whole certification path.

The scope is narrow: service identities based on fully qualified DNS domain names, TLS, DTLS and the older SSL, and PKIX-based systems. Client identities, IP-address identifiers, other security protocols, CA policy, DNS resolution and user interface issues are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Every program used to have its own way of checking the name on a website's ID card. This document gives everyone one common way to do it.

sections.title: The Identifier Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines four identifier types that a certificate can carry for a service.

  • CN-ID: a Common Name in the certificate subject whose value looks like a domain name.
  • DNS-ID: a subjectAltName entry of type dNSName.
  • SRV-ID: a subjectAltName entry of type otherName with the name form SRVName.
  • URI-ID: a subjectAltName entry of type uniformResourceIdentifier with both a scheme and a host component.

Names are classed as direct (given by a user) or indirect (resolved, for example via DNS SRV), and as unrestricted (usable for any type of service) or restricted (usable for one). CN-ID and DNS-ID are direct and unrestricted; SRV-ID is restricted and either direct or, more typically, indirect; URI-ID is direct and restricted.

The domain name part is either a traditional domain name, with only letter-digit-hyphen labels, or an internationalized domain name with at least one U-label or A-label. The subject field may even be empty as long as the certificate has at least one subjectAltName entry. The Common Name is not strongly typed, since it might hold a human-friendly string such as "A Free Chat Service".
sections.eli5: An ID card can write the name in a few different boxes. Some boxes are made exactly for website names, and one old box was never really meant for that job.

sections.title: Rules for Issuers and Requesters
sections.content:
For certification authorities, the key rules are these:

  • The certificate SHOULD include a DNS-ID as a baseline for interoperability.
  • If the protocol calls for them, it SHOULD include an SRV-ID or a URI-ID. For a URI-ID the scheme is that of the protocol and the host is the fully qualified domain name of the service.
  • It SHOULD NOT include a CN-ID unless a reusing specification explicitly encourages continued support. CAs are encouraged to migrate away from putting the domain name there.
  • It MAY hold several DNS-IDs, SRV-IDs or URI-IDs, but SHOULD NOT hold more than one CN-ID.
  • Unless a reusing specification allows it, the domain name SHOULD NOT contain the wildcard character (an asterisk).

For service providers requesting a certificate, the advice is to ask for every identifier type the protocol requires or recommends. A certificate usable for any service type should include only a DNS-ID. To limit a certificate to one service type, add an SRV-ID or URI-ID, and request one certificate per service type rather than one with many SRV-IDs or URI-IDs. Examples include an IMAP server certificate with SRV-IDs _imap.example.net and _imaps.example.net plus DNS-IDs example.net and mail.example.net.
sections.eli5: Whoever makes the ID card should write the website's name in the proper box, and not in the old, fuzzy box. Cards that name a whole street of houses at once should be avoided.

sections.title: How a Client Verifies Identity
sections.content:
Verification has four steps: the client builds a list of reference identifiers from the source domain and, optionally, the service type; the server provides its identifiers in a PKIX certificate; the client checks each reference identifier against the presented ones; and each check matches the domain and, where relevant, the service type.

The client MUST build its list independently of what the server presents. It should use only data that can be securely parsed from the input (such as the host part of a URI) and SHOULD base identifiers on the source domain, not on a derived domain found through DNS. The list SHOULD include a DNS-ID, an SRV-ID if servers for the service are typically found via DNS SRV records, a URI-ID if the protocol uses URIs in certificates, and MAY include a CN-ID for backward compatibility.

Matching rules:

  • Traditional names are compared label by label, case-insensitively. For internationalized names, U-labels are first converted to A-labels.
  • SRV-ID and URI-ID matches must also check the service name or scheme, case-insensitively.
  • The client MUST NOT check a CN-ID if the certificate presents a DNS-ID, SRV-ID, URI-ID or other supported identifier type. Only if none are present MAY it fall back to the CN.
  • A wildcard that is the whole left-most label (*.example.com) matches foo.example.com but not bar.foo.example.com or example.com. Clients SHOULD NOT match wildcards in other labels, or inside an internationalized label.
sections.eli5: Before going anywhere, your computer writes down the name it expects. Then it compares that to the name on the ID card, letter by letter, and only uses the old box if there is no better one.

sections.title: When the Names Do Not Match
sections.content:
If a presented identifier matches, the client MUST use the matched reference identifier as the validated identity. If nothing matches but the user earlier pinned the certificate to one of the reference identifiers and the presented certificate matches the pinned one, the check succeeds.

Otherwise an interactive client SHOULD tell the user about the mismatch and terminate with a bad certificate error, which prevents users from bypassing protection in hostile situations. Letting advanced users pin the certificate is appropriate only in specialized circumstances and needs extreme caution, such as forcing them to view the entire certification path first. An automated client SHOULD terminate with a bad certificate error and log it. It MAY provide a setting to disable this behavior but MUST enable it by default.
sections.eli5: If the name on the card is wrong, a person gets a clear warning and the visit stops. A robot just stops and writes it in its diary.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Wildcard certificates automatically vouch for every host name in their domain, which is convenient but risks vouching for rogue or buggy hosts. Existing specifications also disagree about where a wildcard may appear, and these ambiguities could allow exploitable differences between clients. Nothing defines wildcards inside internationalized labels, so clients are strongly discouraged from attempting them, although a wildcard that fills the entire left-most label is allowed.

Internationalized names can introduce visually similar "confusable" characters. Pinned certificates MUST be remembered together with their context, including the chain to the trust anchor, source domain, service type, derived domain and port number.

Multiple identifiers exist because, in a default TLS handshake, the client cannot say which name it wants and the server returns one certificate. The workaround was to embed many names in one certificate. The Server Name Indication (SNI) extension lets the client state its desired name. The RFC allows several DNS-IDs, SRV-IDs and URI-IDs but says several CN-IDs SHOULD NOT be used, and hopes to tighten this later.
sections.eli5: A card naming every house on the street is risky if one house is bad. And names that look alike can trick people, so everyone should be careful reading them.
